newsitem.title: DEMOCRATIC REPUBLIC OF CONGO: New Congo, Uganda agree joint oil exploration.
newsitem.headline: New Congo, Uganda agree joint oil exploration.

text.p: The Democratic Republic of the Congo and its ally Uganda have agreed to explore jointly for oil in their borderlands, officials said on Tuesday.

Oil exploration around Lake Albert and Lake Edward is one of the regional issues on the agenda of summit talks between Congo's President Laurent Kabila and leaders of Uganda and Rwanda, who helped him seize power in Kinshasa.
Uganda's President Yoweri Museveni arrived in Kinshasa on Monday while Rwanda's Pasacal Bizimungu flew in on Tuesday.
Kabila said at a state dinner for Museveni on Monday that the joint search for oil showed "the time had come for a relaunch of joint projects between the two countries".
"The defunct Republic of Zaire ,which was not interested in joint projects with its neighbours, allowed plans for oil exploitation in the two (lakes) regions to die," Kabila said.
No details of the joint oil project were available.

Having given military support to Kabila's seven-month armed campaign that toppled president Mobutu Sese Seko, land-locked Uganda and Rwanda are sizing up economic benefits in the vast and mineral-rich former Zaire.
Kabila wants to consolidate security around Congo's borders, replacing cross-frontier rebel activity with trade as a means of relaunching his country's moribund economy, his aides say.
"We promise to do everything possible to give the necessary encouragement so that commercial exchanges acroos our frontiers will develope," Kabila said at the dinner.
Museveni said he had discussed security and economic cooperation with Mobutu during three official visits to the ex-Zaire, but the ousted dictator showed no genuine interest.
"I must say that I failed completely because I could not get a single project moving between Uganda and Congo," he said.

"The first item we talked about was security, to try to bring about peaceful conditions in our region. But it never materialised because the old regime kept harbouring elements which were hostile to peace in Uganda," Museveni added.
Mobutu showed no further interest in exploring for oil after the two states signed a draft agreement in 1990, Museveni said.

"That agreement was not even ratified by the Congo, by Zaire that time. So nothing moved. Now all these simple things show you the effective balkanisation of Africa," added Museveni, a vocal champion of pan-African cooperation.

Museveni is seen as a leading strategist in major geo-political shifts taking place in Central Africa since the beginning of the decade. He gave the vital backing to Tutsi rebels who toppled Rwanda's Hutu rulers and army accused of the 1994 genoicide of more than 800,000 minority Tutsis.
The Ugandan leader said the ousting of Mobutu and South Africa's apartheid rulers before that had created the perfect environment for economic cooperation in Afcrica.

"The changes in Congo, the changes in South Africa, the changes in Namibia and the changes in Uganda .. The getting rid of all these wonderful people has got one effect, the effect of actually uniting Africa. So Africa can now start acting together. This is the most important happening that has occured since the end of colonialism," he said.

Museveni defended Kabila against charges that his Tutsi-led rebels massacred Rwandan Hutu refugees who fled to the ex-Zaire as Tutsis took charge in Kigali. He said the refugee centres had been turned into "armed camps" by Hutu hardliners.
"You must stop demonising Mr Kabila because he is not responsible for this," Museveni said.
United Nations investigators are due in Kinshasa this month to look into the massacre charges.
